DETAILED ACTION
Notice of Pre-AIA  or AIA  Status
The present application, filed on or after March 16, 2013, is being examined under the first inventor to file provisions of the AIA .
Information Disclosure Statement
The information disclosure statement (IDS) submitted on 8/25/21 is being considered by the examiner.
Drawings
The drawings are objected to because Figs. 1A, 1B, 2, 3A, 3C, 3D, 5, and 6 appear blurry and are difficult to read. The replacement sheet for Figs. 3B and Fig. 4 are clear and visible. Appropriate correction is required for the blurry and unclear Figs. recited above. Corrected drawing sheets in compliance with 37 CFR 1.121(d) are required in reply to the Office action to avoid abandonment of the application. Any amended replacement drawing sheet should include all of the figures appearing on the immediate prior version of the sheet, even if only one figure is being amended. The figure or figure number of an amended drawing should not be labeled as “amended.” If a drawing figure is to be canceled, the appropriate figure must be removed from the replacement sheet, and where necessary, the remaining figures must be renumbered and appropriate changes made to the brief description of the several views of the drawings for consistency. Additional replacement sheets may be necessary to show the renumbering of the remaining figures. Each drawing sheet submitted after the filing date of an application must be labeled in the top margin as either “Replacement Sheet” or “New Sheet” pursuant to 37 CFR 1.121(d). If the changes are not accepted by the examiner, the applicant will be notified and informed of any required corrective action in the next Office action. The objection to the drawings will not be held in abeyance.
Claim Objections
Claim 17 is objected to because of the following informalities: Applicant is encouraged to delete lines 18-25 after the period since it is repetitive.  Additionally, a claim can only have one period. Appropriate correction is required.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 112
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of 35 U.S.C. 112(a):
(a) IN GENERAL.—The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor of carrying out the invention.
The following is a quotation of the first paragraph of pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112:
The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to which it pertains, or with which it is most nearly connected, to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor of carrying out his invention.
Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.
For the limitation of “deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal” in claim 12, this is a computer implemented functional limitation “source separation algorithm decomposes the abdominal acoustic signal” according to ¶56 of the disclosure. ¶56 of the specification fails to disclose how the machine learning algorithm is used to deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value. MPEP 2161.01(I) states the following:
Claims may lack written description when the claims define the invention in functional language
specifying a desired result but the specification does not sufficiently describe how the function is
performed or the result is achieved. For software, this can occur when the algorithm or
steps/procedure for performing the computer function are not explained at all or are not
explained in sufficient detail (simply restating the function recited in the claim is not necessarily
sufficient). In other words, the algorithm or steps/procedure taken to perform the function must
be described with sufficient detail so that one of ordinary skill in the art would understand how
the inventor intended the function to be performed. See MPEP §§ 2163.02 and 2181, subsection
IV.”
Therefore, the claims with the limitation of “deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal” are rejected under 112(a) for failing to meet the written description requirement.
Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) or 35 U.S.C. 112 (pre-AIA ), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claim(s) contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for applications subject to pre-AIA  35 U.S.C. 112, the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.
For the limitation of “identify a noise correction value” in claims 1 and 17, this is a computer implemented functional limitation “microcontroller is configured to…identify a noise correction value” according to ¶23 of the disclosure. ¶23 and ¶42 of the specification fail to disclose how the comparison creates a noise correction value. This limitation is a functional result without any steps indicating how the result is actually obtained. See MPEP 2161.01(I) above. Therefore, the claims with the limitation of “identify a noise correction value” are rejected under 112(a) for failing to meet the written description requirement. Dependent claims are rejected for the same deficiency set forth for independent claims 1 and 17.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 101
Section 33(a) of the America Invents Act reads as follows:
Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism.
Claim 9 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 and section 33(a) of the America Invents Act as being directed to or encompassing a human organism.  See also Animals - Patentability, 1077 Off. Gaz. Pat. Office 24 (April 21, 1987) (indicating that human organisms are excluded from the scope of patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. 101).
Claim 9 includes the limitation of “a patch that removable attaches to a maternal torso.” As such, the limitation requires that a patch would encompass being in contact with a patient (human organism) under the broadest reasonable interpretation. Applicant should be recommended to change the claimed limitation to –a patch configured to removably attach to a maternal torso-- in order to overcome this 101 rejection.
35 U.S.C. 101 reads as follows:
Whoever invents or discovers any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof, may obtain a patent therefor, subject to the conditions and requirements of this title.
Claims 1-20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101 because the claimed invention is directed to a judicial exception, specifically an abstract idea (mathematical concept of “calculate a first maternal heart rate (mHR) value from the mPCG value and calculate a second mHR value from the mPPG value”  and mental process of “compare the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify a noise correction value”) without significantly more.
Step 1
The claimed invention in claims 1-20 are directed to statutory subject matter as the claims recite a wearable fetal health monitoring device and a method for determining a health condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus.
Step 2A, Prong One
Regarding claims 1 and 17, the recited steps are directed to mathematical concepts and a mental process of performing concepts in a human mind or by a human using a pen and paper (see MPEP 2106.04(a)(2) subsections (I) and (III)).
Regarding claims 1 and 17, the limitations of “calculate a first maternal heart rate (mHR) value from the mPCG value and calculate a second mHR value from the mPPG value” are mathematical calculations of calculating a maternal heart rates in order to apply a noise correct value to the fetal phonocardiogram.
Regarding claims 1 and 17, the limitation of “compare the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify a noise correction value” is a process, as drafted, covers performance of the limitation that can be performed by a human mind (including an observation, evaluation, judgment, opinion) under the broadest reasonable standard. For example, these limitations are nothing more than a medical professional evaluating a noise correction value based on judgement between a first mHR value and a second mHR value.
Step 2A, Prong Two
For claims 1 and 17, the judicial exception is not integrated into a practical application. In particular, claims 1 and 17 recite “a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer, a pulse oximeter, and a microcontroller.” The microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer and pulse oximeter amount to nothing more than pre-solution activity of data gathering. The microcontroller is recited at a high-level of generality and amount to nothing more than a part of a generic computer. Merely including instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer does not integrate a judicial exception into practical application.
Step 2B
The claims do not include additional elements that are sufficient to amount to significantly more than the judicial exception. As discussed above with respect to integration of the abstract idea into
a practical application, the additional elements of a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer and a pulse oximeter amount to nothing more than mere pre-solution activity of data gathering, which does not amount to an inventive concept. Moreover, the MEMS accelerometer and pulse oximeter are recited at a high level of generality and are well-understood, routine, and conventional structures as evidenced by US 20180092564 (¶59-MEMS accelerometer) and US 20170281087 (¶21-pulse oximeter). Further, simply appending well-understood, routine, conventional activities previously known to the industry, specified at a high level of generality, to the judicial exception, e.g., a claim to an abstract idea requiring no more than a generic computer to perform generic computer functions that are well-understood, routine and conventional activities previously known to the industry, as discussed in Alice Corp., 573 U.S. at 225, 110 USPQ2d at 1984 (see MPEP § 2106.05(d)). In this case, elements of general computer are being used to implement the abstract idea.
Regarding dependent claims 2-16 and 18-20, the limitations of claims 1 and 17 further define the limitations already indicated as being directed to the abstract idea.
Claim Rejections - 35 USC § 103
The following is a quotation of 35 U.S.C. 103 which forms the basis for all obviousness rejections set forth in this Office action:
A patent for a claimed invention may not be obtained, notwithstanding that the claimed invention is not identically disclosed as set forth in section 102, if the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art are such that the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious before the effective filing date of the claimed invention to a person having ordinary skill in the art to which the claimed invention pertains. Patentability shall not be negated by the manner in which the invention was made.
The factual inquiries for establishing a background for determining obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 are summarized as follows:
1. Determining the scope and contents of the prior art.
2. Ascertaining the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue.
3. Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.
4. Considering objective evidence present in the application indicating obviousness or nonobviousness.
Claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt (WO 2019133926 filed on 12/28/18) in view of Bureev (RU 2656518 filed on 3/6/14) and Meriheina (US 20180092564 filed on 10/2/17).
Regarding claims 1 and 17, Holt teaches a wearable fetal health monitoring device and method for determining a heath condition of a fetus based on biosignals of an expecting mother and the fetus, the device comprising: a pulse oximeter that generates a maternal photoplethysmogram (mPPG) value from a pulse sensed in the abdominal region (¶6-maternal photoplethysmogram; ¶8-separated signal that corresponds to light incident upon the pregnant mammal (e.g., maternal photoplethysmogram); ¶73-pulse oximetry probe; ¶10-detected optical signal may correspond to an optical signal projected into the pregnant mammal’s abdomen by one or more light sources); calculate a second mHR value from the mPPG value (¶9-secondary signal (e.g. maternal heart rate); ¶8): and compare the first mHR value with the second mHR value to identify a noise correction value (¶75-the maternal heartrate signal may be used to determine which portions of the signals received in step 305 are contributed by the pregnant mammal. These portions may then be subtracted and/or divided from the signals received in step 305 to remove maternal contributions to the signals received in step 305). However, Holt does not teach a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer that converts an acoustic wave sensed in an abdominal region into an abdominal acoustic signal and a microcontroller configured to: generate a maternal phonocardiogram (mPCG) value from the abdominal acoustic signal; calculate a first maternal heart rate (mHR) value from the mPCG; and apply the identified noise correction value to the mPCG value to extract a fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG).
Bureev relates generally to medicine and obstetrics, in particular to medical diagnostics and can be used for mobile monitoring, and monitoring and evaluating the state of the fetus and method (page 4, top of page). Bureev more particularly relates to evaluating with maximum accuracy, the state of the fetus and mother, having a higher quality of registered signals, and increasing reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (page 9, middle of the page). Bureev further teaches the invention using the following steps:
generate a maternal phonocardiogram (mPCG) value from the abdominal acoustic signal (page 6, ¶2-placement on upper and lower part of abdomen of pregnant women, heart tones mother); calculate a first maternal heart rate (mHR) value from the mPCG value (bottom of page 8-heart rate mother); apply the identified noise correction value to the mPCG value to extract a fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value (claim 1-attenuation of external noise and interference before subtracting of registered tones of fetus heart).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include generating a maternal phonocardiogram, a first maternal heart rate, and fetal phonocardiogram of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Meriheina relates generally to monitoring of heartbeats, particularly to monitoring of fetus and infant heartbeats with ballistocardiographic measurements. The present disclosure further relates to an analysis method and an apparatus which allow the weak ballistocardiographic signals caused by infant and fetus heartbeats to be distinguished from more dominant signal components, such as an adult's heartbeat (¶1). Meriheina further teaches a MEMS accelerometer (¶59). Meriheina further teaches the invention using the following steps:
a microelectromechanical system (MEMS) accelerometer that converts an acoustic wave sensed in an abdominal region into an abdominal acoustic signal (¶59-MEMS accelerometer); and a microcontroller (¶57-control unit 26).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include the MEMS accelerometer and microcontroller of Meriheina of the invention in Holt in order to allow the weak ballistocardiographic signals caused by infant and fetus heartbeats to be distinguished from more dominant signal components, such as an adult's heartbeat (Meriheina, ¶1).
Regarding claim 2, Holt teaches a power source operatively coupled to a wireless transceiver (¶25-wireless, power).
Regarding claims 3 and 18, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device and the method of claims 1 and 17. However, Holt does not teach to calculate from the fPCG value at least one of: a fetal heart rate (fHR) value and a fetal heart rate variability (fHRV) value.
Bureev teaches calculating from the fPCG value at least one of: a fetal heart rate (fHR) value (bottom of page 8-heart rate of fetus) and a fetal heart rate variability (fHRV) value (top of page 9-cardiac rhythm variability of fetus).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include calculating from the fPCG value at least one of: a fetal heart rate (fHR) value and a fetal heart rate variability (fHRV) value of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Regarding claim 7, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach calculating a maternal activity level from at least one of the mPPG value and the first mHR value and the second mHR value.
Bureev teaches wherein the microcontroller is further configured to calculate a maternal activity level from at least one of the mPPG value and the first mHR value and the second mHR value (page 5, middle of page-electrical activity of heart mother; bottom of page 8-heart rate mother).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include calculating a maternal activity level from at least one of the mPPG value and the first mHR value and the second mHR value of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Regarding claim 8, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach one or more of: a MEMS inclinometer, an inertia sensor, and a gyroscope.
Meriheina teaches one or more of: a MEMS inclinometer, an inertia sensor, and a gyroscope (¶35-gyroscope; ¶23).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include one or more of: a MEMS inclinometer, an inertia sensor, and a gyroscope of Meriheina of the invention in Holt in order to allow the weak ballistocardiographic signals caused by infant and fetus heartbeats to be distinguished from more dominant signal components, such as an adult's heartbeat (Meriheina, ¶1).
Regarding claim 9, Holt teaches a patch that removably attaches to a maternal torso (¶46- an adhesive designed to be applied to the skin of the pregnant mammal’s abdomen (e.g., glue, tape, etc.) configured to apply housing 102/fetal hemoglobin probe 1 15 directly to the skin of the pregnant mammal’s abdomen and hold it in place there in a manner similar to a sticker).
Regarding claim 16, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach a noise attenuator configured to: at least partially constructively or destructively combine a first physiological signal component of a first signal output by a first acoustic sensor and a second physiological signal component of a second signal output by a second acoustic sensor.
Bureev teaches a noise attenuator configured to: at least partially constructively or destructively combine a first physiological signal component of a first signal output by a first acoustic sensor and a second physiological signal component of a second signal output by a second acoustic sensor (claim 1-attentuation of external noise and interference; page 7, middle of page-combined in one housing with complex acoustic sensors 1 and 2).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date that the claimed invention include a noise attenuator configured to: at least partially constructively or destructively combine a first physiological signal component of a first signal output by a first acoustic sensor and a second physiological signal component of a second signal output by a second acoustic sensor of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Regarding claim 19, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the method of claim 17. However, Holt does not teach outputting at least one of a normal state, caution state, and emergency state based on the extracted fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value.
Bureev teaches outputting at least one of a normal state, caution state, and emergency state based on the extracted fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value (page 5, top of page- monitoring the fast changes of the state of the fetus; page 8, ¶2-emergency mode; page 6, ¶2-tones of the fetus heart; page 7, middle of page-digital or an analog output, is intended for recording tones of fetus heart).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective filing date that the claimed invention include outputting at least one of a normal state, caution state, and emergency state based on the extracted fetal phonocardiogram (fPCG) value of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Claims 4 and 20 are rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Igney (US 20100305481 filed on 5/7/08).
Regarding claims 4 and 20, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device and the method of claims 1 and 17. However, Holt does not teach calculating a fetal movement (fM) value from the abdominal acoustic signal.
Igney teaches calculating a fetal movement (fM) value from the abdominal acoustic signal (¶17-movements of the fetus)
Igney relates to a system and method for automatically monitoring the movement activity of a fetus (¶1). Igney additionally teaches an easy and completely unobtrusive way of monitoring the movement activity of an unborn child. With the present invention the evaluation and monitoring of child movements can be carried out completely automatically in a home environment (¶16).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include calculating a fetal movement (fM) value from the abdominal acoustic signal of Igney of the invention in Holt in order to provide an easy and completely unobtrusive way of monitoring the movement activity of an unborn child. With the present invention the evaluation and monitoring of child movements can be carried out completely automatically in a home environment (Igney, ¶16).
Claim 5 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Venugopalan (US 20170049414 filed on 5/22/15), hereinafter referred to as Ven.
Regarding claim 5, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach wherein the pulse oximeter is further configured to sense a maternal peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (mSpO2) value.
Venugopalan teaches wherein the pulse oximeter is further configured to sense a maternal peripheral capillary oxygen saturation (mSpO2) value (¶35-maternal pulse oximetry (SpO2); ¶43).
Ven relates generally to providing wireless sensor. More specifically the subject matter relates to a wireless sensor capable of communicating with a remote ultrasound processing system for managing fetal and maternal data (¶1). Ven also relates to the fetal and maternal data being examined by a medical practitioner to determine the health status of the fetus and the subject (¶6). Ven further teaches the maternal pulse oximetry (SpO2) (¶35).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include the mSpO2 value of Ven of the invention in Holt in order to provide a wireless fetal sensor and system for managing fetal data and maternal data of a subject, so that the fetal and maternal data can be examined by a medical practitioner to determine the health status of the fetus and the subject (Ven, ¶6).
Claim 6 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Stahmann (US 7787946 filed on 9/1/04).
Regarding claim 6, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach wherein the MEMS accelerometer comprises at least one of an acoustic wave sensor and a pressure wave sensor.
Stahmann teaches wherein the MEMS accelerometer comprises at least one of an acoustic wave sensor and a pressure wave sensor (col. 238 and lines 19-28-accelerometer based acoustic sensors, MEMS-based acoustic sensors).
Stahmann relates generally to systems and methods providing patient monitoring, diagnosis and/or therapy (Field of the Invention section). Stahmann further teaches one or more functions of two or more individual medical procedures may be used in combination to enhance patient monitoring, diagnosis and/or therapy (col. 2 and lines 52-54).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include wherein the MEMS accelerometer comprises at least one of an acoustic wave sensor and a pressure wave sensor of Stahmann of the invention in Holt in order for one or more functions of two or more individual medical procedures may be used in combination to enhance patient monitoring, diagnosis and/or therapy (Stahmann, col. 2 and lines 52-54).
Claim 10 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Workman (US 20170281087 as cited in the IDS and filed on 3/31/17).
Regarding claim 10, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach wherein the device comprises two units spaced apart from each other, wherein the two units are carried on a belt or band that surrounds a maternal torso.
Workman teaches wherein the device comprises two units spaced apart from each other, wherein the two units are carried on a belt or band that surrounds a maternal torso (¶20-the belly-covering garment 140 may comprise a belt or a stray that is capable of holding the sensor modules sensor modules 120(a-d) adjacent to the belly 100; Fig. 1).
Workman relates generally to a system for monitoring fetal health data and/or mother health data. Workman further teaches a belly-covering garment that is configured to at least partially cover a belly and to hold one or more sensor modules directly adjacent to the belly (¶5). Workman additionally teaches determining whether the fetus is within the first region or the second region based upon readings received from the first sensor module and the second sensor module (¶7).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include wherein the device comprises two units spaced apart from each other, wherein the two units are carried on a belt or band that surrounds a maternal torso of Workman of the invention in Holt in order to determine whether the fetus is within the first region or the second region based upon readings received from the first sensor module and the second sensor module (Workman, ¶7).
Claim 11 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Zia (US 20140180153 filed on 12/23/13).
Regarding claim 11, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach an acoustic impedance matching housing.
Zia teaches wherein the device further comprises an acoustic impedance matching housing (¶32-acoustically impedance matched, housing).
Zia relates generally to medical diagnostic systems, and more particularly, to a system and method for acoustic detection of coronary artery disease and automated editing of heart sound data (¶3). Zia also teaches systems and methods for adaptively canceling noise in an acoustic heart signal and/or automatically editing heart sound data (¶10).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include an acoustic impedance matching housing of Zia of the invention of Holt in order for adaptively canceling noise in an acoustic heart signal and/or automatically editing heart sound data (Zia, ¶10).
Claim 12 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Chen (WO 2018148251 filed on 2/7/18).
Regarding claim 12, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach wherein the microcontroller is further configured to deconvolute the abdominal acoustic signal using at least one of the first mHR value and the second mHR value.
Bureev the abdominal acoustic signal (page 6, ¶2-placement on upper and lower part of abdomen of pregnant women, heart tones mother) using the first mHR value (bottom of page 8-heart rate mother).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include the abdominal acoustic signal and using the first mHR value of Bureev of the invention in Holt in order to evaluate with maximum accuracy the state of the fetus and mother, have higher quality of registered signals, and increase reliability and diagnostic value of produced data (Bureev, page 9, middle of the page).
Chen teaches wherein the microcontroller is further configured to deconvolute (¶98-deconvoluting mixed signals with respect to the identified sources, heart sound).
Chen relates generally to a methodology is disclosed that enables calculation of the systolic and diastolic blood pressures continuously in a non-invasive manner, based on the heart sounds measured from the chest of a human being (¶47). Chen also teaches deconvoluting mixed signals (¶98).  Chen also teaches analyzing acoustic signals, locating and separating noise sources via multi-channel microphones as an effective approach for both airborne and structural-born noise problems (¶99).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include the deconvolution of Chen of the invention in Holt in order analyze acoustic signals, locate and separate noise sources via multi-channel microphones as an effective approach for both airborne and structural-born noise problems (Chen, ¶99).
Claim 13 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Ransbury (US 20180317789 filed on 5/2/18).
Regarding claim 13, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach an inclinometer sensor that detects a sub- audible abdominal acoustic wave.
Ransbury teaches an inclinometer sensor that detects a sub-audible abdominal acoustic wave (¶37-inclinometer; ¶30-acoustic waveforms; ¶31-sub-audile frequencies).
Ransbury relates generally to methods and systems for remote monitoring of heart activity (¶2). Ransbury more particularly relates to a wearable heart monitoring device for monitoring heart activity comprising one or more acoustic sensors, including at least one microphone configured to operate in a frequency range related to human hearing, and at least one accelerometer configured to operate in the range of low or sub-audible frequencies (¶4).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
filing date that the claimed invention include an inclinometer sensor that detects a sub- audible abdominal acoustic wave of Ransbury of the invention in Holt in order to operate in the range of low or sub-audible frequencies and analyzing the data collected by the one or more sensors to determine a condition of a heart (Ransbury, ¶9).
Claim 14 is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina as applied to claims 1-3, 7-9, and 16-19 above, and further in view of Khine (US 20170086709 A1 as cited in the IDS and filed on 5/18/15).
Regarding claim 14, Holt in view of Bureev and Meriheina teaches the device of claim 1. However, Holt does not teach wherein a first portion of the device is disposable, and wherein a second portion of the device is re-usable.
Khine teaches wherein a first portion of the device is disposable, and wherein a second portion of the device is re-usable (¶70-a disposable patient interface; ¶95-reusable component).
Khine relates generally to a wearable sensor for monitoring fetal movement (e.g., fetal kicks) and/or health. The disclosure relates to technology for monitoring fetal health during later stages (e.g., weeks 24+) of pregnancy. More specifically, a sensor can be worn by a mother to extract biometric data about the fetus. This data can be used as an indirect indicator of fetal health (¶9). Khine further teaches that this wearable sensor is less cumbersome then existing technology to improve user compliance. With continuous monitoring a decline in fetal movement can be detected earlier then without this device (¶10).
Therefore, it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art before the effective
